data.title: Trump defends ties with Putin as Russia intensifies attacks on Ukraine
data.description:
By Josh Wingrove and Hadriana Lowenkron
 
President Donald Trump defended his relationship with Vladimir Putin, repeatedly insisting that the Russian leader wants to end the war in Ukraine despite Moscow’s latest deadly assault. 
“He’d love to end the war. It’s a very hard thing to do, to be honest,” Trump said during a White House press briefing on Friday. 
 
Trump has hailed his meeting this week with Putin in Shenzhen, China as a success, calling the Russian leader “my friend” and saying their discussions will help bring peace, even as Russia’s war nears its five-year mark. He declined, however, to say whether Putin is a friend of the US.
 
 
“I can’t speak to America,” Trump said. 
 
Trump acknowledged it is challenging to end the conflict he vowed to resolve at the start of his term, pointing to the “tremendous hatred” between Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. On Friday, Trump said any discussion of security guarantees the US would offer Ukraine — necessary for Kyiv to accept any peace agreement — was premature, declining repeatedly to say if Washington was prepared to offer Nato-like security guarantees to Ukraine in any deal.
 
“I don’t want to talk about security guarantees because we got to get a deal first,” he said. “So when we have a deal, we’ll be involved because we want to.”
 
The president’s son in law, Jared Kushner, who has been working toward a peace deal, said Thursday Trump was open to strong security guarantees and Trump has said he would not make any agreements with Putin without input from Ukraine despite having cast Zelenskyy as the bigger obstacle to peace.
 
That murky dynamic has left Ukraine and its allies uneasy as the US ramps up efforts to broker an end to the war, exacerbating fears that Trump will pressure Kyiv to accept unpalatable territorial or security concessions or open up negotiations on the continent’s overall collective security arrangements. Discussions on the broader security posture across Europe are considered a non-starter for Ukraine’s allies until Russia halts the fighting.
 
Hours after Trump met one-on-one with Putin in China — their first sit-down in more than a year — Russia carried out one of its largest attacks on Ukraine, killing eight people and injuring nearly 30. Zelenskyy said the strikes caused outages of electricity, water and heating in Kyiv and other parts of the country.
 
The attack followed Putin’s threat to forcefully retaliate for a Ukrainian strike that damaged a key bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea. The Russian leader also ruled out the prospect of a partial truce.
 
“I can only tell you that President Putin would like to get this settled,” Trump said, “Now I don’t know if he wants to say that because maybe it’s not his negotiating, you know, right to say that. But he would like to get this settled, and I think it will be settled.”
 
Putin has continued attacks targeting Ukrainian cities and civilians and has demanded Kyiv hand over territory his military has been unable to control on its own. 
 
European allies were skeptical of Trump’s assessment of his talks with Putin after the US president called into a gathering of Ukrainian allies in Berlin on Thursday. 
 
“His faith in Putin’s good will seems unwavering, although no facts confirm this at this time,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told reporters.
 
Putin on Thursday said he had invited European officials to Moscow to discuss the war, opening a door to negotiations. Officials from the E3 group of France, Germany and the UK have also been discussing a possible meeting with Moscow, Bloomberg reported earlier.

data.title: Jensen Huang should return as Nvidia CEO after 'big apology', says Trump
data.description:
By Josh Wingrove and Courtney Subramanian
 
President Donald Trump called for Jensen Huang to make a big apology and return as chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp., even as the prospect remains highly unlikely. 
The Nvidia board has indicated they don’t intend to bring back the embattled former CEO, but Trump on Friday continued to insist that the return would be a good idea because he is “one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world.”
 
He reiterated at a White House press conference that his own pick to replace Huang is Apple Inc.’s Tim Cook but added that he “would love to see Jensen be given a second chance. You know we’re a country of second chances.”
 
 
“I’d like to see Jensen make a big apology and go back,” Trump said. “He put us in a position where we are literally 10 years advanced over other companies.” 
 
While Trump joins Silicon Valley figures close to Huang, including billionaire Elon Musk, in calling for the former CEO’s return, the board has dismissed the idea and interim CEO Colette Kress looked to reassure staff at a town hall about the company’s future after the ouster. 
 
Allegations in a California lawsuit filed in 2007 show that Nvidia employees’ complaints about how Huang treated his staff — including allegations that he threatened them and made sexually explicit remarks — date back decades.
 
Trump said he discussed the Nvidia matter with Chinese President Xi Jinping during a meeting in Shenzhen earlier this week, saying his counterpart also called Huang “brilliant.” The US president also compared Huang to Musk, saying he was “very proud of protecting Elon in my first term” and that he continues to do “pretty amazing” things. 
 
The revelations that Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who worked at a Singapore-based firm that obtained advanced chips from his company loomed over the leaders’ sitdowns. 
 
That tumult allowed infighting among US administration officials over China policy and the enforcement of curbs on semiconductor exports to spill into the open, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent openly blaming the Commerce Department, led by Secretary Howard Lutnick, for not acting to prevent China from obtaining the advanced technology.  
 
Bessent cited Commerce’s failure to add the Singapore-based firm, Megaspeed International, to the entity list that would have cut it off from sensitive US technology. Lutnick also has been called to testify before Congress about his relationship with Nvidia. 
Trump has continued to back Lutnick despite the criticism, asserting Friday in response to a question that he had not lost confidence in his Commerce secretary. He told reporters on Monday before leaving for his four-day trip to the Philippines and China that Lutnick had “done a very good job” and may have stalled restrictions to avoid further conflict with Beijing.
 
Amid the scrutiny, the Commerce Department on Monday sought to limit several countries from providing Chinese companies remote access to advance AI chip and servers, a move likely to anger Beijing and regional partners. China has warned the US over those restrictions, and Beijing is seen to be already mulling some retaliation.
 
The US president has repeatedly dismissed concerns that the fallout from the Nvidia scandal compromised US national security, telling reporters before his trip, “China plays games with us, and we play games with China.”

data.title: Cyclone Akvan: Odisha's Mayurbhanj, Balasore under red alert for heavy rain
data.description:
Odisha Revenue and Disaster Management Minister Suresh Pujari on Friday said Mayurbhanj and Balasore districts have been placed in the red zone following a reassessment of the weather situation after Cyclonic Storm Akvan made landfall near Gopalpur in Ganjam district.

Pujari said the cyclone had crossed the coast and was moving towards the north and northwest at a wind speed of 55 to 65 kmph, while gradually weakening. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued a red warning for Mayurbhanj and Balasore, an orange warning for several other districts and a yellow warning for the remaining parts of the state.

"The latest position is that the landfall of the Cyclonic Storm Akvan took place near Gopalpur of the district of Ganjam at around 10:30 to 11:00 a.m., and in the meantime, it has already crossed the coast and is moving towards the north and northwest at a speed of 55 to 65 kmph wind speed, and it is becoming weak," Pujari said.

 

He said the IMD had reassessed the warning levels for different districts.

"As a result, the IMD has reassessed the danger level of different districts, and they have now put Mayurbhanj and Balasore in the Red Zone, and other districts like Keonjhar, Bhadrak, Jajpur, Dhenkanal, Kendrapara, Jagatsinghpur, Nayagarh, Cuttack, Khordha, Puri, Kandhamal, Gajapati, and Ganjam in the Orange Zone, and the rest of the districts of Odisha in the Yellow Zone," he said.

Pujari added that the red zone districts were likely to receive heavy to very heavy rainfall, while other parts of the state under the yellow warning could also experience rainfall over the next 24 hours.

Meanwhile, Mayurbhanj district has been placed under a red alert, with continuous heavy rainfall making the situation critical, particularly during night hours, Additional District Magistrate Netrananda Mallick said.

Senior district officers are closely monitoring the situation across 12 flood-prone and vulnerable blocks. Cooked food is being distributed to people sheltered at flood relief centres.

Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force (ODRAF) teams, along with fire services personnel, remain on high alert and have been deployed at three locations in the district to respond to emergencies. Authorities are monitoring the evolving weather conditions and are prepared to intensify relief and rescue operations if required.

In Bhadrak, Odisha Minister Suryabanshi Suraj said 26,173 people had been relocated, and 145 relief camps had been set up in the district.

"...26,173 people from Bhadrak district have been relocated. 145 relief camps have been set up...Bhadrak received an average of 50.86 mm of rainfall yesterday and only 15.29 mm today. The situation is under control," Suraj said.

data.title: CERT-In flags unauthorised payment transactions, warns of AI cyberattacks
data.description:
India's cyber agency said on Friday it had reported unauthorised transactions at service providers ​for banking and financial services entities, ​and also at technology service providers supporting government-linked payments.

Payment fraud incidents extended beyond the financial sector to vendors and partner payout platforms, cyber agency CERT-In said in an advisory on Friday.

Attackers altered business records or approval relationships and then used legitimate payment processes, it said. It did not say how much money had been improperly paid out, or by whom.

The agency ‌also said that it identified the use of AI-driven frameworks in cyberattacks across different sectors, and issued several recommendations for government organisations, non-financial payout platforms and technology service providers.

 

India has seen a spate of cyberattacks on banks and non-bank lenders ​in recent weeks, even as authorities issued warnings and the Reserve Bank of ‌India tightened cybersecurity checks.

Earlier this month, CERT-In named the hacking group behind a ​wave ‌of AI-driven attacks on financial firms and identified its tools, ‌at least two of them linked to China.

Late last month, India's central bank warned banks ‌of ​rising cyberattacks on ​financial infrastructure, seeking proof of compliance with existing rules and details of their preparedness for ‌AI-related risks.

data.title: Nvidia employees accused Huang of abusive conduct in 2007 lawsuit
data.description:
By Brian Baxter (BLAW), Maggie Eastland and Ian King
 
About two decades ago, two Nvidia Corp. employees complained about how then-Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang treated his staff, including allegations that he threatened them and made sexually explicit remarks, according to allegations contained in a California lawsuit filed in 2007. 
Stephen Pettigrew, the first in-house lawyer hired by Nvidia, said he observed Huang regularly verbally abusing and intimidating employees, according to court documents filed in the Superior Court of California. Pettigrew alleged he was fired for raising concerns about the conduct of Nvidia executives, while the company cited performance issues for his termination, according to court documents.
 
 
“He would scream at them, threaten them with extreme bodily harm and make sexually oriented comments while thrusting his hips in a demonstration of the sex act,” according to a brief filed by Pettigrew’s attorneys in a lawsuit alleging age discrimination and wrongful termination. The dispute, in which Nvidia brought counterclaims against Pettigrew seeking the return of corporate documents, was resolved through a confidential settlement in December 2009.
 
Another employee, Michael Winston, the senior vice president for human resources, filed a discrimination complaint in 2005 alleging he was fired after objecting to “Huang’s abusive treatment of employees, including conduct he believed constituted sexual harassment,” according to court documents from Pettigrew’s lawsuit, which contain some details from Winston’s complaint.
 
The behavior of Nvidia’s founder toward his employees, even decades ago, is front of mind for many as he appeals to the board to let him return to the position he occupied for more than three decades. He resigned earlier this month following disclosures of multiple affairs including with a direct report and a suspected Chinese spy whose relationship with Huang is being investigated by the US Justice Department. Huang himself has admitted to “torturing” those who work closely with him to make sure they deliver their best work, and news stories have surfaced about him allegedly demeaning subordinates during his extended tenure running the company.
 
He has never fought characterisations of being harsh and has, at times, publicly shown that side of his personality. 
 
A representative for Huang said, “These false allegations are from over 20 years ago and were made by two fired employees. The thousands of employees who have shown support for Jensen over the last week show they are false.”
 
Nvidia representatives didn’t respond to requests for comment. Details of the complaints were previously reported by the New York Times.
 
Huang, 63, has explained his approach as being motivated by a sense of crisis and needing to move forward quickly in a rapidly changing technology industry. He has often expressed his pride in not laying off staff and regretted the one time he did so. 
Some of his Silicon Valley allies are supporting the effort to reinstate Huang, and so are some Nvidia employees, according to an anonymous poll that says it reflects their responses. So far, the board and senior management have publicly rejected the prospect Huang coming back.
 
In the vast majority of his appearances outside of Nvidia or at events open to the public, he behaves in a congenial, often lighthearted and joking way and makes time for people. While he was at Nvidia, those who reported to him maintained a reverential demeanor when discussing him, even while admitting that he could be fearsome.
 
Both Pettigrew and Winston are deceased, and several attorneys representing them and family members couldn’t be reached for comment.
 
A former electrical design engineer who previously worked at three large law firms, Pettigrew joined Nvidia in September 1999 after the company went public earlier that year. He was fired in June 2006.
 
In his lawsuit, Pettigrew sought more than $2.6 million in damages from Nvidia, and the company at one point tried to settle the case for $175,000, according to court records. In the court filings, Pettigrew described wrongdoing by an unnamed “senior executive at Nvidia” who allegedly made sexual remarks and threatened to rip off an employee’s arm off and beat them with it. The executive also allegedly said, “If that’s your business plan, then bend over and drop your pants.”
 
A trial brief in Pettigrew’s case cited the discrimination complaint filed by Winston, which Pettigrew received from California’s Department of Fair Employment and Housing while working for Nvidia in 2005, according to court records. Depositions in Pettigrew’s case stated that Winston, who was hired by Nvidia in September 2004, spent only four weeks at the company. 
 
Nvidia reached a confidential settlement agreement with Winston for more than $1 million, according to the New York Times.
 
Winston would subsequently make a name for himself as a would-be corporate whistleblower, with a jury awarding him $3.8 million in damages from Countrywide Financial Corp. after he claimed the company fired him for raising concerns about its lending practices. A federal appeals court overturned that award.

data.title: Anthropic researcher claims AI helped solve 150-year-old Riemann hypothesis
data.description:
By Elena Eisenstadt and Rachel Metz
 
On the heels of Anthropic PBC’s record-breaking initial public offering, a researcher at the company said he believes he used its artificial intelligence software to solve a famous number theory problem that has plagued mathematicians for more than 150 years. 
Mathematician Levent Alpöge published a note on his personal website on Friday, claiming to have come up with a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. He shared a link to code written in the programming language Lean that he said showed evidence of his success. 
 
According to his note, Alpöge messaged Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei on Sunday night to ask about announcing his findings to the public. Alpöge called the timing of his announcement “horrible,” but said, “I just could not live if I waited even longer.” Anthropic declined to comment, and Alpöge did not respond to a request to comment.
 
 
The Riemann hypothesis relates to the distribution of prime numbers and has long been considered one of the most difficult math problems in the field.
 
OpenAI and Anthropic have been working for years to demonstrate the advanced capabilities of their most cutting-edge models by solving challenging math and life sciences problems. 
 
If confirmed, Alpöge’s work would mark the second Millennium Prize Problem that may have been solved by AI; OpenAI said its models had generated a solution to the 90-year-old Navier-Stokes problem in September. 
 
Andrew Sutherland, a senior research scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said he verified Alpöge’s work about the Riemann hypothesis on his computer and has seen at least three other verifications on multiple systems from other professional mathematicians.
 
Alpöge’s efforts with Claude build on the work of many mathematicians who have studied the Riemann hypothesis, as well as the field of mathematic formalization, according to Sutherland.
 
“I am both very nervous and very excited” for the future, Sutherland said, explaining that mathematicians have years ahead to dig into this proof to understand how it can be applied. “This is a day for celebration,” Sutherland said, even as he acknowledged the concerns in his field about AI’s potential impacts the math profession and other jobs.
 
Noah Giansiracusa, an associate professor of math at Bentley University and faculty associate at Harvard University, added that, if the solution works, it’s a big deal for AI.
 
“It sounds like there’s a pretty good chance this is airtight and valid,” Giansiracusa said.
 
Alpöge described the experience of attempting to prove the problem as a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt.” 
 
“Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line,” Alpöge wrote.

data.title: Delhi AQI remains 'poor' at 279, six stations record 'very poor' air
data.description:
Delhi's air quality remained in the 'poor' category on Saturday, with the national capital recording an overall Air Quality Index (AQI) of 279 at 7 am, according to the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB). Several monitoring stations across the city, however, reported air quality in the 'very poor' category.
 
Aiims recorded the highest AQI among the monitoring stations cited, at 369, followed by Chandni Chowk at 365. Wazirpur registered an AQI of 332, while Anand Vihar recorded 327. IIT Delhi and Bawana reported readings of 308 and 304, respectively, placing all six locations in the very poor category.
 
Among other monitoring stations, R K Puram recorded an AQI of 274, while Narela registered 245. IGI Airport (T3) recorded 242, followed by Dwarka Sector 8 at 241 and Najafgarh at 236. These locations remained in the poor category.
 
 
According to CPCB's classification, an AQI of 0-50 is considered good, 51-100 satisfactory, 101-200 moderate, 201-300 poor, 301-400 very poor and 401-500 severe. While the city's overall reading remained in the poor category, the station-level data indicated considerably worse conditions in several neighbourhoods.
 
The deterioration comes days after the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) revoked Stage III restrictions under the Graded Response Action Plan (Grap) in Delhi-NCR on November 17, citing an improvement in air quality.
 
The CAQM's sub-committee on Grap withdrew the restrictions with immediate effect. Following the decision, all government, government-aided and recognised private schools in Delhi were directed to resume physical classes for students.
 
However, the withdrawal of Stage III restrictions did not mean that all pollution-control measures were lifted. The authorities continued to be responsible for implementing measures under the lower stages of Grap.
 
Meanwhile, Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta has called for intensified efforts to tackle pollution, directing departments to coordinate their actions and ensure visible results on the ground.
 
At a high-level review meeting at the Delhi Pollution Control Committee's Integrated Command and Control Centre earlier this week, Gupta said the capital had experienced some relief in November compared with the past decade. She, however, stressed that the government would continue taking strict action against sources of pollution.
 
The chief minister directed the Municipal Corporation of Delhi and the Public Works Department to intensify mechanised sweeping, water sprinkling and road washing to control dust on roads, footpaths and central verges.
 
She also called for stricter inspections at construction and demolition sites, directing officials to ensure the installation of green nets, barricades and windbreakers. Dust-control measures, she said, should not be treated as a mere formality.

data.title: India Inc must summon the courage to challenge government policy openly
data.description:
The most apt description for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s mass admonition of corporate India at the Ficci annual general meeting is that it was a cri de coeur.
 
I use this even as I’m reminded of the late and venerable D N Singh, my first news editor at The Indian Express in 1977. He had banned “foreign” words in our writing. English is foreign enough for all of us, he’d say.
 
In this case, however, a cry from the heart doesn’t fully capture where the Prime Minister was coming from. The dictionary tells us that a cri de coeur is more profound. It’s a “passionate, heartfelt appeal, protest, even an outcry”. The Prime Minister spoke in anger, frustration, helplessness even. What more can I do to get you guys moving? It was way more fraught than a mere cry from the heart.
 
 
It’s a bit like a general failing to implore his troops to assault a hill despite a thousand war cries, words of inspiration, even a dash of “spirit”. Since we started with a bit of French, that “spirit” reference is from the Duke of Wellington at the Battle of Waterloo.
 
While his original line, as recorded in history, was less dramatic, Christopher Plummer, playing Wellington in the 1970 film Waterloo, tells the Duchess of Richmond, who wants to know where his troops get their inspiration to fight: “Gin is the spirit of their patriotism.” I’m avoiding the full quote because the Prime Minister certainly didn’t want to call corporate India ‘scum, beggars and scoundrels,’ as Wellington called his troops. It’s just that his frustration is as profound.
 
What’s the spirit that a government can offer entrepreneurship? It can be many things: Deregulation, minimum government, fair market supervision, fiscal discipline, freedom from licensing and investment restrictions. And certainly, the gin equivalent of this “spiritual” package would be tax cuts.
 
One big cause of Mr Modi’s frustration is corporate India’s unwillingness to pass this benefit on to employees through raises, hiring or investment. This hasn’t happened even as corporate profits have risen. These troops are unwilling, either too scared to assault that hill or simply too comfortable in safety, pocketing the tax breaks. Let’s read some of Mr Modi’s words to Ficci.
 
“In 2014, the basic corporate tax rate was 30 per cent. We reduced it to 22 per cent. Today, there’s no income tax on earnings up to ~12 lakh in India.” And then he turns the knife.
 
“I know you won’t clap, because however much one gives, your appetite never seems to be satisfied. (aap ka pet nahin bharta). Did you increase the salaries of your employees? Did you increase the number of employees? No. The attitude remains: ‘Modi ji, you do it, we will see’.”
 
While India Inc was left licking its wounded pride, the Congress quickly latched on to the Prime Minister’s words. Isn’t this what we’ve been saying all along, it hit back. Jairam Ramesh was first out of the blocks. “For the first time in 12 years, a nervous and rattled PM has pulled up the captains of industry... (who) must have been taken aback and shocked.” In an elaborate post on X, he blamed not businesses but the government for this stall.
 
He blamed it on crony capitalism, regulatory capture, “an atmosphere of fear and intimidation”, and the unleashing of “investigative agencies”. He concluded by suggesting the Prime Minister look inwards. Rahul Gandhi, on his speaking tour in the United States, also said: We told you so.
 
It’s not my place here to hold forth on the state of the economy. But we know corporate India hasn’t been investing, expanding and hiring, at least nowhere near what 7 per cent-plus growth would indicate. Startups are rising, but largely there’s an entrepreneurship freeze. Much of the growth comes from government spending, especially in heavy infrastructure.
 
If corporate India looks so risk-averse, this isn’t a sudden development. The mood has been festering for years. Some complain of a lack of demand, others say regulation is asphyxiating. Still too many forms need to be filled for too many small things, even something as virtuous as exports. Because, I suppose, the Reserve Bank of India wants to track every dollar that comes in. And, of course, everything in triplicate please.
 
The government may have loosened policies here and there, but the bureaucratic grip is tighter than before.
 
A quick quiz, and no Googling. Can you name the ministers of mines, pharmaceuticals and steel? I mention these three because the Prime Minister highlighted corporate India’s failures specifically in these areas. Why do we export raw materials like iron ore, have so much bauxite, yet import finished steel and specialised aluminium alloys? How come, despite robust pharma exports, we remain dependent on China for APIs, or active pharmaceutical ingredients? With key ministers too lightweight or distracted by party work, and power centralised in the PMO, which is obviously far too overburdened to attend to everything, discretion devolves to the bureaucracies. Corporate India is resigned to this.
 
It’s buying peace in the manner it knows best: Distributing some of the spoils in a way that’s entirely legal and above board, but also revealing. Check out the number of retiring secretaries, especially in the finance ministry, finding sinecures on the boards of influential companies and as chairpersons of almost all significant private-sector banks, and the recently listed stock market titan, NSE (National Stock Exchange).
 
The more the Modi government thinks it’s reforming — and reforming it is — the more it does so in a way that passes power into the hands of the bureaucracy. Corporate India buys peace with them in advance, merely by dropping hints. Here’s the paradox. This is a super-strong government with a very weak implementation spine. As a result, what’s decentralised at the top gathers in the middle.
 
A strong government isn’t immune to policy confusion. On the contrary, it can be prone to flip-flop-flips given its overwhelming power. Long term capital gains (LTCG) tax is a big discussion point now. Count how many changes this government has brought in. The same goes for taxes on dividends.
 
Since 1991, successive finance ministers have said that the essence of a reformed economy lies in moderate, predictable taxes. You most certainly cannot say the same about this government, which also taxes individuals at almost twice the rate of corporations. It’s also been breathtaking in its use of sovereign power. A striking example is the retrospective changes it made to sovereign gold bonds to suit itself and cover for those brilliant people who floated these without hedging for gold prices. The message is an old one. In India, the government, the almighty Sarkar-e-Hind, can never be wrong.
 
Corporate India has a lot to answer for, but for some, the chappal is on the government’s foot. On copper and aluminium imports, two of the largest projects have been shut under activist pressure. If this government has failed to move on these, it cannot blame India Inc.
 
Sadly, corporate India knows this, but nobody would dare speak up. They whisper dark things on the sidelines. But in front of an angry Prime Minister, or the finance minister who’s been delivering the same admonitions for two years, they sit silent and contrite, like schoolkids whose homework the dog ate.
 
This isn’t just a Modi-era phenomenon. At the 2007 CII AGM, then Prime Minister Manmohan Singh had chided corporate leaders for paying themselves too much. The irony: The mood and message then were opposite to now. Sunil Mittal, then CII chief, responded by pledging ‘a significant part of his salary bonus’ to charity.
 
I had then written, and repeated in a 2013 column, that corporate India has to grow the spine to tell the Prime Minister he didn’t fix their wages. He should leave them alone if they paid their taxes honestly. Of course, no such thing happened. Corporate India also swallowed that retrograde idea of near-mandatory corporate social responsibility.
 
Even at Ficci, and in the corporate and financial universe, too many good people have too many important points to make. But nobody would dare. Corporate India is waiting for its next Rahul Bajaj. Or preferably a few of them.
 
By special arrangement with ThePrint

data.title: China's nuclear buildup is 'hot and heavy', says Trump day after meeting Xi
data.description:
Beijing is building nuclear weapons at a "hot and heavy" pace, President Donald Trump said, a day after he met Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin and the three countries agreed to talks on preventing nuclear proliferation.

While Russia and the US lead the world by each possessing thousands of nuclear weapons, China is rapidly expanding its nuclear arsenal.

In its annual review of China's military buildup, the Pentagon said China's stockpile of nuclear warheads remained in the low 600s through 2024, but the country was on track to have more than 1,000 warheads by 2030.

"They'll catch us within 10 years," Trump said of China's nuclear buildup during a news conference at the White House on Friday. "They're going at it hot and heavy, but they have a lot." Trump's public remarks were his first since his controversial summit with Xi and Putin, leaders of countries long considered US rivals, in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen on Thursday. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who spoke to reporters alongside Trump on Friday, said it was imperative for the three nuclear powers to talk.

 

"These three countries possess the overwhelming majority of nuclear weapons on this planet," Rubio said. "The idea that these three leaders should not engage on a regular basis is not just absurd, it's dangerous." After the trilateral meeting, the leaders issued a joint statement, saying they "affirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and "will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons".

Prior to the meeting, observers had doubted if China would agree to nuclear talks. With a much smaller nuclear arsenal, Beijing had resisted joining nuclear arms control talks with the US and Russia.

data.title: Anthropic's IPO attracts $120 billion in retail demand, surpassing SpaceX
data.description:
By Anthony Hughes
 
Anthropic PBC’s initial public offering drew roughly between $115 billion and $120 billion of demand for shares from retail investors, according to a person familiar with the matter, more than the amount sought by them in SpaceX’s debut.  
The frontier AI lab’s first-time share sale had well over $500 billion of demand from institutional investors, more than double the orders for shares in SpaceX, the person said, asking not to be identified as the information isn’t public.
 
Anthropic’s IPO is the biggest of all time, with the $93.5 billion raised by the company and its seven co-founders, including the over-allotment, comfortably topping SpaceX’s $86.2 billion offering. Anthropic also raised $26 billion in a private placement, for a total haul of $119.5 billion. 
Even as the IPO delivered a record amount to the company, adding to the nearly $132 billion of cash and equivalents it had as of Sept. 30, Anthropic’s shares erased much of their first-day jump on Friday, testing investors’ faith after the AI lab delivered the biggest initial public offering in history.
 
 
Shares of Anthropic fell as much as nearly 15 per cent on Friday, after the stock gained 17 per cent in its first trading day as a public company. The trading gives Anthropic a market value of about $1.5 trillion, ranking it among the 15 biggest publicly traded companies in the world.
 
Most of the stock in Anthropic’s IPO went to long-only investors and sovereign wealth funds, with venture capital investors receiving a low-to-mid single digit percentage point share in aggregate, the person said. Banks working on the first-time share sale, led by Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and Morgan Stanley, allocated fewer shares to investors relative to the size of the offering than those who placed orders for SpaceX’s IPO, they said.
 
Retail investors in Anthropic’s IPO received about 15 per cent of the shares available, Bloomberg News reported. 
 
Some of the details of the demand were previously reported by the International Financial Review and the Financial Times. Representatives for Anthropic, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley declined to comment.
 
SpaceX’s IPO maintained its dominance in some corners of the retail universe. Demand for Anthropic’s IPO was second to SpaceX’s first-time share sale, still the record-holder on both Robinhood Markets Inc. and Charles Schwab Corp.’s platforms. 
 
More than 360,000 people requested shares in the Anthropic IPO through Robinhood Financial and Trade PMR, and everyone who requested a share received at least one, if not more, a Robinhood spokesperson said. AI-related shares led activity on Schwab’s platform on Friday, with Anthropic among the top five names, according to a Schwab spokesperson.
 
Anthropic’s IPO left more than half of the institutional investors bidding for stock without any shares, with allocations heavily skewed toward US-based investors, Bloomberg News reported. About 1,200 institutional investors placed orders, people familiar with the matter have said. 
The company sold $1.1 billion worth of stock to retail investors in the UK and continental Europe, and raised about $3 billion in Japan and around $110 million in Australia, Bloomberg News has reported.
 
The 22 banks on Anthropic’s IPO earned a record $550 million in fees for their work, more than on SpaceX’s IPO. They didn’t receive fees for the so-called over-allotment shares, or for the private placement shares, according to its filings.
 
Demand for SpaceX shares ran to more than $350 billion, with over $100 billion coming from retail, people familiar with the matter said at the time.
 
Anthropic’s listing joins companies linked to AI that have lifted US IPO volume to an all-time high. First time stock sales raised $258 billion this year, beating 2021’s $195 billion haul, excluding financial vehicles such as blank-check firms, data compiled by Bloomberg show. 
 
Anthropic won over investors with a focus on enterprise customers, propelling its run-rate revenue — a measure annualized from a shorter period — to $81 billion as of Oct. 31, up $10 billion from the end of September, its regulatory filings show.
 
Claude Code, the company’s coding agent for software developers, is widely adopted in the industry and has even been used by NASA engineers, the filing shows. Anthropic has more than 11,900 customers delivering $100,000 of revenue each on a trailing 12-month basis as of the end of September, up from about 1,500 in 2025.
 
Anthropic and its rival OpenAI face mounting public scrutiny over AI safety after a string of high-profile hacking incidents by rogue agents, and as the debate rages over whether the technology poses what Anthropic called “existential risks to humanity” in its IPO filing. OpenAI has filed confidentially for a listing but isn’t planning to go public before 2027.
